title: Surrender
tomorrow: Pop calls the cane one more thing to wear. what goes on last?

segments.voice: That was a week of the heart: a stranger who turned back, a crowd that feasted after tears, a prisoner who learned contentment, a farmer who waits, a leader told be strong, a father who wouldn't despair. Yesterday's line: hope holds.

Can you pray please fix it and whatever you want in the same breath? Jesus did. Night on the Mount of Olives. He tells his friends to pray, goes on about a stone's cast, and kneels. And the first thing he asks for is honest, and very human: that what's coming might not come.
screen: `PLEASE FIX IT. WHATEVER YOU WANT.` → `NIGHT, ON THE MOUNT OF OLIVES.` → `HE ASKS FIRST.`

segments.voice: Luke gives the prayer: “Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.” The cup is the suffering ahead. Notice the order. He asks first, and he means it. Surrender here isn't pretending not to want anything. It's saying plainly what you want, then letting go of the outcome. The hinge is one word: nevertheless. Mark keeps the word Jesus opened with, Abba, the family word for father, so the letting go happens inside trust, not fear. And it echoes a prayer he taught his followers in daylight: thy will be done. Now look back at the week, because surrender gathers it up. Gratitude turns back. Joy feasts after tears. Contentment stays steady. Patience waits and keeps tending. Courage takes one step in company. Hope holds out of sight. Each one asks honestly for something, then opens its hands. Christians describe this scene in different words: obedience, trust, or simply yes.
screen: `HE ASKS FIRST: REMOVE THIS CUP.` · `NEVERTHELESS.` · `ABBA: INSIDE TRUST.` · `THE WEEK, WITH OPEN HANDS.` · then, large: `THY WILL.`

segments.voice: Name one outcome you're gripping: a result, a reply, someone else's choice. Say honestly, in your head, what you want. Then turn your hands palms up on your knees and rest them there; if you pray, you can use his words: not my will, but thine, be done.
Surrender. Saying honestly what you want, then letting go of the outcome in trust.
Your line: thy will. Said after an honest ask, not instead of one. Seven days of the heart, done.

howItsDone: Christians pray 'thy will be done' in the Lord's Prayer, and some recall Jesus' prayer on the Mount of Olives when facing outcomes they cannot control; some pray it with open hands.

fork.setup: a friend's dad just lost his job. she says, 'i'm just going to accept it and not ask God for anything.' what does the prayer on the Mount of Olives suggest?
options: ask honestly for what you want, then trust God with the outcome.
never ask; real surrender means wanting nothing at all.
keep demanding until it changes, and don't let go.
fork.reveal: Jesus asked first, “remove this cup from me,” and then said “nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.” the ask comes before the letting go.

chat.says: pop needs a cane for a long while. he calls it 'one more thing to wear.' hope or surrender?
options: Both. Hope holds on; surrender asks honestly, then lets go.
Surrender. Hope is for people who won't accept facts.
Hope. Surrender would mean he's stopped trying to walk.
chat.meaning: Hope holds out of sight; surrender, in the garden, asks first and then says thy will. They work together: holding on to good, letting go of control.

Mount of Olives.meaning: a hill just east of Jerusalem's walls

cup.meaning: here, the suffering that lay ahead of him

Abba.meaning: Aramaic for father, the family word

nevertheless.meaning: even so; the turn in Jesus' prayer
